title: Oops, I Contaminated It Again: Investigating Cross-Contamination in Liquid Cell TEM via Correlative Operando Electrochemistry and Cryogenic Atom Probe Tomography
content: Liquid cell transmission electron microscopy (LCTEM) is a powerful microscopy technique that allows for real-time, high-resolution imaging of nanoscale processes in liquid environments. This has provided unprecedented insights into various dynamic nanoscale processes such as nanomaterial synthesis, corrosion, electrochemical phenomena, and biological systems [1]. LCTEM is typically achieved using a closed cell set up, involving a top and bottom silicon wafer chip with printed silicon nitride membrane windows to view the region of interest, in combination with a liquid supply system or syringe pump system [2, 3]. This allows liquid to flow through the system of interest while being imaged and remain unaffected by the vacuum of the TEM column. Often due to the immense cost of a LCTEM system, these types of setups in research settings can be shared across multiple research groups using different solvents and different samples of interest for different applications. LCTEM manufacturers outline extensive cleaning procedures to ensure cross contamination does not occur when switching experiments/solvents. However, it is an impossible task to determine if absolutely no contamination is present even following routine cleaning.
